methods.label: Compare the two base triangles
methods.explanation:
The equal base angles let us compare triangles \(BDF\) and \(CEF\) without finding any individual angle. Let \(t=\angle ABC=\angle ACB\), since \(AB=AC\). Every angle of equilateral triangle \(DEF\) is \(60^\circ\).

Because \(A,D,B\) are collinear, the angles at \(D\) give
\[
\angle BDF=180^\circ-b-60^\circ=120^\circ-b.
\]
The angle sum in triangle \(BDF\) is therefore
\[
t+a+(120^\circ-b)=180^\circ,
\]
so \(b=t+a-60^\circ\).

Similarly, \(B,F,C\) are collinear, so
\[
\angle EFC=180^\circ-a-60^\circ=120^\circ-a.
\]
The angle sum in triangle \(CEF\) gives
\[
c+t+(120^\circ-a)=180^\circ,
\]
so \(c=a+60^\circ-t\).

Adding the expressions for \(b\) and \(c\) eliminates the unknown base angle:
\[
b+c=(t+a-60^\circ)+(a+60^\circ-t)=2a.
\]
Thus \(\boxed{a=\dfrac{b+c}{2}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
